facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus is an extinct genus of eusuchian crocodylomorphs found in the Eastern United States during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Eothoracosaurus (meaning "dawn Thoracosaurus") is an extinct monospecific genus of eusuchian crocodylomorphs found in Eastern United States which existed during the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The holotype of Eothoracosaurus, a skull and postcrania, was discovered in 1931 and formally described by Kenneth Carpenter in 1983.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Eothoracosaurus (MSU 3293, a skull and associated postcrania in the collection of the university's Dunn-Seiler Museum) was originally discovered in 1931 and first described by Kenneth Carpenter in 1983 and initially referred to Thoracosaurus neocesariensis.

facts.statement: Christopher Brochu reexamined the material in 2004 and established the separate genus Eothoracosaurus due to substantial differences from other thoracosaurs.
facts.quote: The material was eventually reexamined by Christopher Brochu in 2004, taking note of substantial differences to other thoracosaurs and finding them severe enough to warrant a separate genus: Eothoracosaurus.

facts.statement: The name Eothoracosaurus combines "Thoracosaurus" with the prefix "eos" meaning dawn, reflecting its earlier appearance in the fossil record compared to its relative.
facts.quote: The name derives from the genus Thoracosaurus (chest lizard) and the prefix "eos" meaning dawn, chosen to reflect the fact that Eothoracosaurus appeared earlier in the fossil record than its relative.

facts.statement: The species name mississippiensis refers to the state of Mississippi, where the holotype was found.
facts.quote: The species name mississippiensis represents the state of Mississippi, where the holotype was discovered.

facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus had a strongly elongated skull similar to the modern gharial, which grew notably broader towards the back of the head.
facts.quote: Like in the modern gharial, the skull of Eothoracosaurus is strongly elongated with the head growing notably broader further back.

facts.statement: Each premaxilla of Eothoracosaurus contained 5 teeth, where the first four were roughly equal in size and the fifth was notably smaller.
facts.quote: Each premaxilla contains 5 teeth, with the first four roughly equal in size while the fifth is notably smaller.

facts.statement: The maxillae of Eothoracosaurus contained 21 to 22 teeth on each side.
facts.quote: The maxillae contain 21 to 22 teeth on each side.

facts.statement: The preserved teeth of Eothoracosaurus were slender, conical, and fairly evenly spaced.
facts.quote: The preserved teeth show they were slender and conical and fairly evenly spaced.

facts.statement: In Eothoracosaurus, the frontal process of the nasal bone was twice as long as the main body, distinguishing it from Thoracosaurus where the ratio was closer to 1:1.
facts.quote: In Eothoracosaurus, the frontal process is twice as long as the main body, while in Thoracosaurus the ratio is closer to 1:1.

facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus is associated with marine environments and coastal habitats, likely living in and around shallow marine areas.
facts.quote: Thoracosaurs such as Eothoracosaurus are typically associated with marine environments and coastal habitats and are thought to have lived in and around shallow marine areas.

facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus likely fed on fish and cephalopods.
facts.quote: They are likely to have eaten fish and cephalopods.

facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Eothoracosaurus is classified within the family Gavialidae.
Eothoracosaurus belongs to the class Reptilia.

facts.statement: Research by Boerman et al. (2026) interprets the endocranial anatomy of Eothoracosaurus as consistent with a marine ecology and a lack of capability for deep diving.
facts.quote: Boerman et al. (2026) reconstruct the endocranial cavities of Thoracosaurus isorhynchus and Eothoracosaurus mississippiensis, and interpret their anatomy as consistent with marine ecology and lack of capability of deep diving.

rejected.statement: Traditionally, thoracosaurs like Eothoracosaurus were thought to be related to the modern false gharial because their nasal bones contact the premaxillae, but later studies placed them within the gavialoid lineage.
rejected.quote: Thoracosaurs in general were traditionally thought to be related to the modern false gharial, largely because the nasal bones contact the premaxillae, but phylogenetic work starting in the 1990s instead supported affinities within gavialoid exclusive of such forms.
